A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Plan-R1 work and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures. The supplied v1 ends after its references despite mentioning an appendix; v3 includes Appendices A-D. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original nuPlan closed-loop experiments, a pretraining-versus-fine-tuning ablation, and KL-weight and pass@k analyses in Section 4.

after.justification: V3 reports original nuPlan results and optimizer, world-model, capacity, group-size, and reward-component experiments in Section 4 and Appendix B.

M1.justification: V3 introduces VD-GRPO, replacing per-group standard-deviation normalization with mean centering and fixed scaling. Section 3.3 also changes the stated fine-tuning objective from trajectory-level likelihood ratios and advantages to token-level ratios with cumulative advantages. The autoregressive backbone and frozen-world-model/trainable-ego design already existed in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions use nuPlan urban trajectory planning, the Val14, Test14-random, and Test14-hard splits, and reactive and non-reactive closed-loop evaluation. V3's additional ablations and visualized scenarios remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: The external comparator roster in Table 1 is unchanged. Standard GRPO, previously the proposed optimizer, becomes an explicit comparator for VD-GRPO in v3 Table 2. Table 3 additionally evaluates doubled-capacity pretraining and ground-truth-replay controls.

E3.justification: The main protocol retains 1M pretraining instances, 100K fine-tuning scenarios, and 15-second simulations at 10 Hz. New ablations vary model capacity, rollout world model, group size G=2/4/6, and scaling constant c; the KL sweep extends to smaller weights. Table 2 expands the earlier reactive-score comparison to report both NR-CLS and R-CLS.

E4.justification: V3 adds GRPO-versus-VD-GRPO ablations, advantage-distribution and unsafe-group training diagnostics, and controls testing reactive world modeling against replay and increased capacity. Appendix B adds group-size, scaling-constant, and reward-removal studies, while Appendix A adds rollout visualizations. The KL and pass@k analyses already existed in v1 and are revised and moved to Appendix B.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V3's advantage histograms and rollout-group sizes concern optimizer behavior and sampling design, rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces both Plan-R1 result rows under the retained benchmark settings. Without post-processing, Test14-hard R-CLS changes from 73.18 to 77.20 and Test14-random R-CLS from 88.89 to 90.04; with post-processing, Test14-random R-CLS decreases from 94.51 to 93.71. These results concern the revised planner. Numerous ablation results are added, and the KL/pass@k curves change numerically. V3 leaves the pass@k evaluation subset unspecified, limiting direct comparison of those curves.

T1.justification: Formal revisions are concentrated in the optimization definitions: v3 Equations 3-5 introduce stepwise rewards, cumulative token advantages, and fixed-c scaling in place of v1's trajectory-level GRPO formulation. The joint-distribution factorization and conditional-independence assumptions remain equivalent. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The two-stage principle-alignment and nuPlan performance claims remain. However, v3 adds a central claim that standard GRPO suppresses rare safety-critical signals and presents VD-GRPO as a contribution addressing this failure. This substantially expands the paper's claimed contribution beyond applying rule-based GRPO fine-tuning.

C2.justification: V1 mainly attributes improvements to reinforcement-learning exploration and explicit principle alignment. V3 adds a detailed explanation of how group normalization dilutes safety signals, qualifies standard GRPO's benefits through its collision-score deterioration, and interprets world-model/capacity controls and reward-removal experiments. Appendix B also adds explanations of group-size and scaling/regularization tradeoffs.

D1.justification: V3 Appendices C-D supply previously unavailable reward weights, bounding-box collision checks, reward-to-token assignment, vocabulary and architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, training epochs, hardware, and top-1 inference details. The abstract also adds a code-availability statement and repository link. These are substantial documentation additions; they do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

R1.justification: V3 substantially repositions the work around hybrid imitation/reinforcement learning and GRPO's safety-specific limitations. Section 2 adds discussion of BC-SAC, DAPO, and Dr.GRPO, explicitly acknowledging inspiration from Dr.GRPO while distinguishing the planning objective. This replaces v1's broader trajectory-language-modeling and sequence-fine-tuning positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method explanations are extensively rewritten. Related work changes from three subsections to two, the contribution narrative centers on VD-GRPO, and the KL/pass@k discussions move from the main ablation section to Appendix B. These changes substantially reorganize the exposition beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: V3 updates Figure 1's optimizer/world-model labeling, expands Table 2, and adds Tables 3-5 and Figures 4-6 and 9. V1's KL and pass@k plots are redrawn and relocated as v3 Figures 8 and 7; Figures 2-3 largely retain their visual content. Typography, citation presentation, and page layout also change throughout.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially improves reproducibility through Appendices C-D and strengthens the safety mechanism's empirical support through optimizer diagnostics and world-model, capacity, and reward ablations, addressing important gaps in v1. These gains outweigh localized new errors: Table 2 reports a drivable-score gain of 2.64 although its entries imply 2.68, and Appendix B incorrectly says increasing c amplifies gradients despite Equation 5 dividing by c. The improvement rests on stronger documentation and evidence, rather than uniformly higher scores.
